items.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: I put Bill Holman writing the Artie Shaw thing because Bill had that melodic kind of thing.

ctx.x: That was just a fluke. It was the biggest fluke. I recorded a band in New York in 1956 or something like that and I was sick because it wasn’t good — not to me, it wasn’t good. I used the same rhythm section that was with my little group. I always try to use the guys who travel with me and kill themselves on the road, to give them a good job. If I did a T.V. show, I was steadily using a quartet, three of the guys from the house band, I want my guys on there. I always tried to push them on there. So I put them on…

idea was I was going to hire six different arrangers and pay tribute to six different band leaders, like Duke Ellington, Lionel Hampton, Count Basie, Tommy Dorsey, Benny Goodman and Artie Shaw. And I was going to take something out of each arrangement, like Artie Shaw’s clarinet chorus on “Stardust” just the first 16 bars, and somewhere would sneak it in the arrangement, or part of Ben Webster’s chorus on “Cottontail,” whatever, you know. And I hired the arrangers that I thought would write for those guys. I put…
But they want you in the studio.

items.title: Holman Bill — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: So he said, “We‟ll do the album, use the charts to play on the gig – on our in-person gig.” So we did that.

ctx.x: We talked about an early recording with him, but let‟s talk about that tenure with him.

In ‟59 he was working at a club called the Seville down on Santa Monica Boulevard with his quartet. He said – he asked the leader one night. He said, “How would you like a big band to come in here and work all week long for the same money you‟re giving me?” The owner said sure. So Terry, the ultimate businessman, he put all these things together. He had a contract with Mercury to make a big band album. So he said, “We‟ll do the album, use the charts to play on the gig – on our in-person gig.” So we did that. I…

come up with the funniest tunes. One of them was – I think on the first album – was Tico Tico. I think of a lady organ player on The Hit Parade that used to play that, and they‟d always shoot her feet on the pedals. But a jazz chart on Tico Tico? Uh-uh. But I did it, and it came off okay. I wrote some of my best things for that band, I think, in strictly a jazz band vein. Terry – again, the businessman – he wanted a big chord on the end of every chart, whether it called for it or not, regardless of what the song…
